strengths: Addresses a well-motivated practical problem: joint (rather than separate) pre-training of camera and LiDAR encoders is blocked by GPU memory constraints, and the paper proposes concrete mechanisms (curvature sampling) to overcome this.

The overall pipeline is a coherent combination of differentiable-rendering-based masked reconstruction with a SwAV-style swapping prototype assignment scheme, extended with an EM optimization step and gram-matrix regularization to avoid prototype collapse.

Experiments include a main comparison on NuScenes with BEVFusion, an ablation study isolating the contribution of joint pre-training, curvature sampling, and prototype learning, a scaling study across different label fractions, qualitative visualizations of curvature and prototype assignments, and a supplementary cross-dataset transfer experiment to Once with CenterPoint.

The idea of computing curvature from the SDF normal field to guide informative point/pixel sampling for masked rendering is a reasonably novel and intuitive contribution for reducing computational cost while retaining useful signal.
weaknesses: The headline '300% more improvement' claim is a relative comparison on very small absolute gains (2.48% vs 0.72% mAP; NDS improvement of UniPAD is only +0.01, essentially noise), which is a misleading way to frame the result and raises questions about whether the UniPAD baseline was properly tuned/reproduced in this joint-training comparison.

Only one prior pre-training method (UniPAD) is used as a baseline, despite multiple other unsupervised fusion pre-training methods being cited in related work (SimIPU, CALICO, etc.); none of these are empirically compared, weakening the claim of state-of-the-art performance.

Main results are only reported on a single downstream detector (BEVFusion) and only in a few-shot fine-tuning regime (5%, 2.5%, 1%, 0.5% labels); no full-dataset fine-tuning results are shown, which is standard practice and would clarify whether gains persist with abundant labeled data or diminish.

The ablation shows that naive joint pre-training with uniform sampling actually underperforms the separately-pretrained UniPAD baseline (49.55 vs 49.81 mAP), suggesting the joint training procedure itself may be unstable or suboptimal, and that curvature sampling is compensating for a self-inflicted problem rather than purely adding value.

Curvature is estimated from the second derivative of an SDF predicted by a network that is simultaneously being trained from scratch, which is likely to be extremely noisy, especially early in training; the paper only partially addresses this with a short warm-up phase and provides no quantitative validation of curvature estimation accuracy, only qualitative visualizations with cherry-picked 'good' and 'noisy' examples.
No quantification of the actual GPU memory savings or compute trade-offs achieved by curvature sampling versus using all points/pixels, despite this being the central motivating problem of the paper.

No error bars, multiple random seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported; given the modest absolute performance margins (often 1-3 mAP points), results could plausibly be within run-to-run variance.

Limited technical novelty: the core components (SwAV-style prototype swapping, EM clustering, gram-matrix regularization, differentiable rendering) are largely adopted from prior work (SwAV, UniPAD, NeuS) with incremental combination rather than fundamentally new methodology.

The Once transfer experiment uses a LiDAR-only detector (CenterPoint) rather than a fusion detector, which does not directly validate the paper's central claim about improving fusion 3D perception via joint multimodal pre-training in a cross-dataset setting.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: the GPU memory bottleneck that has prevented joint (rather than separate) pre-training of camera and LiDAR encoders via differentiable rendering, which is a reasonable and practically motivated research direction.

The combination of curvature-based informative sampling with a SwAV-style swapping prototype prediction loss, augmented by an EM step and Gram-matrix regularization to avoid prototype collapse, is a reasonably novel engineering combination for this specific joint pre-training setting.
Qualitative visualizations (curvature heatmaps, prototype assignment maps) provide some intuitive support that the proposed sampling and prototype mechanisms are behaving as intended.

Includes a cross-dataset transfer experiment (NuScenes-pretrained weights applied to Once with CenterPoint) and a LiDAR-only downstream detector, which somewhat broadens the evidence base beyond the single main setting.
weaknesses: The headline '300% more improvement' claim is a relative comparison of very small absolute gains (UniPAD +0.72% mAP vs CLAP +2.48% mAP on one dataset/detector/label-fraction combination); this framing is misleading and the underlying absolute improvement is modest and not clearly shown to be statistically significant (no repeated runs, error bars, or variance reported).

Only a single directly comparable baseline (UniPAD) is evaluated experimentally, despite the related-work section discussing several other multi-modal/fusion unsupervised pre-training methods (SimIPU, CALICO, 2D-3D neural calibration, PonderV2); none of these are run as baselines, making the SOTA claim weakly supported.

All main results rely on a single dataset (NuScenes) and a single downstream fusion detector (BEVFusion); the only diversification (Once + CenterPoint) is LiDAR-only and reported in the supplementary with even smaller gains (0.5–2.4%), which further undercuts the significance of the proposed joint pre-training benefit.

The ablation study is very coarse (only 4 rows, one component added at a time) and does not disentangle the contributions of the three prototype-learning sub-losses (SwAV loss, EM loss, Gram matrix regularization) or the two sampling components (LiDAR curvature sampling vs. pixel sampling), leaving the necessity of each design choice largely unverified.

The ablation shows that naively enabling joint pre-training with random sampling actually hurts performance relative to separate pre-training (49.81 → 49.55 mAP), which is only briefly mentioned and not analyzed in depth; this raises concerns about the robustness/reproducibility of the joint training pipeline itself.

The central motivating claim—that curvature sampling and the proposed pipeline solve the GPU memory problem enabling joint pre-training—is not substantiated with any concrete memory/runtime/batch-size measurements comparing separate vs. joint pre-training, despite this being framed as a primary contribution.

The 'potential scaling property' analysis in Table 2 does not actually scale up the pre-training data (the paper explicitly states pre-training data could not be scaled); instead it shrinks the fine-tuning label fraction, which is a weaker and somewhat indirect proxy for the claimed scaling behavior.

The paper's writing contains multiple typos and inconsistent notation/grammar (e.g., 'hight GPU memory', 'seperate', duplicate variable naming for signed distance and color value s), suggesting insufficient polish for a top-tier venue.

No comparison of computational cost (pre-training time, memory footprint) between CLAP and UniPAD is provided, despite efficiency being central to the paper's motivation, making it hard to assess whether the added complexity (prototypes, EM, Sinkhorn iterations, curvature computation) is a worthwhile trade-off.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical problem: enabling joint (rather than separate) unsupervised pre-training of camera and LiDAR encoders under GPU memory constraints, which is a clear limitation of the SOTA UniPAD approach.

Curvature Sampling is a reasonably novel and intuitive idea for selecting informative points/pixels, with a clear geometric derivation (SDF-based normal and curvature estimation) and supporting visualizations.

The combination of swapping prototype assignment prediction with an EM refinement step and a Gram-matrix regularization to avoid prototype collapse is a sensible adaptation of SwAV-style ideas to the cross-modal 3D setting.
Ablation study clearly isolates the contribution of joint pre-training, curvature sampling, and prototype learning, showing each component adds incremental value.

Additional cross-dataset transfer experiments (pre-train on NuScenes, fine-tune CenterPoint on Once) and scaling-ratio experiments (varying fine-tuning data fraction) add some evidence of generality and practical usefulness.
Prototype visualization qualitatively supports the claim that prototypes capture some object/background semantics in an unsupervised manner.
weaknesses: The headline '300% more improvement' claim is relative to an already very small UniPAD gain (0.72 mAP), which is somewhat misleading framing; the absolute improvement of CLAP (2.48 mAP) is still modest for a computationally heavier joint pre-training pipeline.

Despite the paper's core motivation being GPU memory/computational feasibility, there is no quantitative comparison of actual memory consumption, batch size, or training throughput between CLAP and separate pre-training (UniPAD) to substantiate the central claim.

Main results rely on a single downstream detector (BEVFusion) and a single dataset (NuScenes) for the primary comparisons; only one additional detector/dataset (CenterPoint/Once) is used for transfer, limiting generality claims.
No error bars or multiple-run variance reported, which is concerning given the few-shot fine-tuning regime (0.5%-5% labels) where results can be noisy.

Missing comparisons against other fusion-oriented unsupervised pre-training baselines beyond UniPAD (e.g., contrastive cross-modal methods like SimIPU/Calico mentioned in related work), making it hard to judge CLAP's standing relative to the broader literature.
Key hyperparameters (number of prototypes NK, Sinkhorn iterations, warm-up epochs) are not ablated, so their sensitivity/robustness is unclear.

The curvature estimation relies on the SDF network that is itself being trained, and visualizations show non-trivial noise; there is limited quantitative analysis (only qualitative visualization) of sampling quality versus alternative informative-sampling heuristics.

No direct empirical evidence (e.g., prototype similarity statistics with/without the Gram Matrix loss) is shown to demonstrate that collapse would actually occur without the proposed regularization, weakening support for that specific design choice.
Minor writing/typo issues (e.g., 'hight' in the abstract, 'seperate' in table captions) suggest the manuscript could benefit from a careful proofreading pass.

strengths: First work to enable joint (rather than separate) differentiable-rendering-based pre-training of image and LiDAR encoders for fusion perception, addressing a real computational bottleneck (GPU memory) that previous SOTA (UniPAD) could not overcome.

The curvature sampling strategy is a well-motivated and reasonably novel idea, grounded in the intuitive observation that flat surfaces are less informative than high-curvature regions; the method is theoretically justified via SDF second-order derivatives and empirically validated via visualization (Fig. 4) and ablation (Table 4).

The prototype learning framework (EM training, swapping prediction loss, Gram matrix regularization) is a coherent and reasonably novel adaptation of SwAV-style clustering to bridge cross-modal 3D representations, with clear ablation showing each component's incremental contribution.

Extensive experiments across two major AD datasets (NuScenes, Waymo), multiple downstream detectors (BEVFusion, CenterPoint), and several baselines (ALSO, OCC-MAE, SLidR, PPKT, UniPAD) with consistent, non-trivial improvements (up to 100% higher mAP gain vs. prior SOTA).

Careful experimental protocol addressing convergence bias (training from-scratch models until convergence before comparing to pre-trained fine-tuning), which is a good practice often skipped in the pre-training literature.

Rich supplementary experiments (semantic segmentation transfer, repeated evaluation for robustness, cross-dataset transfer to Once, prototype visualization) that meaningfully strengthen the claims of generality and robustness beyond the main paper.
Potential scaling property analysis (varying fine-tuning data fraction) provides some evidence of the pre-training method's data efficiency benefits, relevant for practical low-label regimes.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains are relatively modest in absolute terms (e.g., ~2.5% mAP on NuScenes, ~1.3% average on Waymo); the '100% more improvement' framing, while technically accurate as a relative comparison to UniPAD's small gains, may overstate practical significance given UniPAD's baseline gain itself was small (near saturation/noise level in some metrics).

No standard deviation or repeated trials are reported for the main results tables (Tables 1-4), except for a single repeated-evaluation experiment relegated to the appendix on a different setting; this makes it hard to assess statistical significance of the main comparisons.

The prototype learning module's contribution (50.81 -> 51.17 mAP, Table 4) is fairly small relative to the curvature sampling contribution (49.55 -> 50.81), raising questions about how much of the 'joint pre-training + cross-modal interaction' story is actually driving results versus the sampling strategy alone.

The paper does not report computational overhead/training time comparisons against separate pre-training (UniPAD) in the main text, which is important given the core motivation is computational efficiency; only a rough per-epoch time is given in the appendix without comparison baselines.

Curvature estimation relies on differentiating a partially-trained SDF network especially early in training, and the visualization (Fig. 4) shows notable noise in the estimated regions; there is limited quantitative analysis of how sampling quality affects final results beyond the single ablation row.

The number of learnable prototypes (NK=512) and their semantic interpretability are only qualitatively visualized (color-coded point clouds) without quantitative validation (e.g., correlation with object categories or purity metrics), so the claim that prototypes meaningfully represent 'parts of 3D scenes' is not rigorously substantiated.

Related work discussion on fusion 3D object detection and contrastive learning is somewhat generic and could better clarify the precise technical delta versus PonderV2/Ponder and other neural-rendering pre-training works beyond UniPAD.

Some experimental design choices (e.g., single random seed for main tables) and reliance on fixed hyperparameters without sensitivity analysis (e.g., number of prototypes, warm-up epochs, temperature) limit reproducibility confidence and understanding of robustness to these choices.

strengths: Addresses a real and practical limitation of prior differentiable-rendering-based pretraining (UniPAD), namely the inability to jointly process point clouds and images due to memory constraints, and proposes a plausible mitigation (curvature-based sampling).

The overall pipeline (curvature sampling + prototype learning with EM, swapping prediction, and Gram matrix regularization) is a coherent, if incremental, combination of existing ideas (SwAV-style prototypes, Sinkhorn assignment, NeuS-style rendering) adapted to a new joint multimodal pretraining setting.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across two standard benchmarks (NuScenes, Waymo) with multiple baselines, and appendix experiments (semantic segmentation, repeated-seed evaluation, cross-dataset transfer to ONCE) that show some consistency of the small gains.
Ablation study isolates the contribution of curvature sampling vs. prototype learning, and qualitative visualizations of curvature/prototype assignments are provided for intuition.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains are small (e.g., +2.48 mAP on NuScenes 5%, +1.28 average on Waymo 1%), and the headline claim of 'up to 100% more improvement' is a misleading relative comparison against baselines whose own gains are tiny (e.g., UniPAD +1.12 vs CLAP +2.48), which inflates the perceived significance of a marginal absolute effect.

The ablation shows that naive joint pre-training (row 2, Table 4) actually performs worse than the separate-pretraining baseline (49.55 vs 49.81 mAP), meaning the core motivating claim of the paper -- that jointly exploiting complementary modalities is beneficial -- is only realized once curvature sampling and prototype learning are added; this weakens the narrative that joint pretraining per se unlocks mutual benefit and raises concern about the fragility/sensitivity of the approach.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: curvature-based importance sampling and SwAV-style prototype/Sinkhorn/EM machinery are well-established techniques individually; their combination here, while reasonably engineered, does not represent a substantial conceptual advance.

No direct wall-clock/memory comparison against the separate-pretraining baseline is provided to substantiate the central claim that curvature sampling meaningfully solves the computational bottleneck (only a rough epoch time is mentioned in the appendix, without baseline comparison).

Evaluation is restricted to low-data few-shot fine-tuning settings (5% NuScenes, 1% Waymo); it is unclear how benefits scale with more fine-tuning data or larger downstream models, and full-data results are not reported in the main text.

Baseline comparisons, while covering several methods, omit some more recent or stronger fusion-based self-supervised approaches, and comparisons are run under the authors' own re-implementation/settings, raising reproducibility concerns about fairness of comparison.

Statistical robustness is only checked via repeated seeds for a subset of results (Appendix, NuScenes only) with a single downstream detector/dataset combination; broader significance testing (e.g., Waymo, ONCE) is missing.
The writing and notation are dense and at times redundant (e.g., repeated explanations of experimental protocol), which affects clarity and readability without adding substantive content.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical bottleneck (GPU memory) that has prevented joint image-LiDAR pre-training via differentiable rendering, and proposes a reasonably well-motivated solution (curvature sampling) grounded in a geometric intuition (SDF second-order derivatives to estimate surface curvature).

The prototype learning framework (EM training, swapping prediction loss, Gram matrix regularization) is a coherent and non-trivial adaptation of clustering-based self-supervised ideas (e.g., SwAV) to the cross-modal 3D fusion setting, with a clear explanation of how it differs from the original single-modality formulation.

Extensive empirical validation: results on both NuScenes and Waymo, an ablation study isolating the contribution of joint pre-training, curvature sampling, and prototype learning, a scaling study varying fine-tuning data ratio, semantic segmentation transfer, cross-dataset transfer to Once, and repeated-run statistics (mean/std) for robustness.
Good use of visualizations (curvature heatmaps, prototype assignment maps) that qualitatively support the claimed mechanism of the method.

Comparisons against a reasonably comprehensive set of relevant baselines (ALSO, Occupancy-MAE, SLidR, PPKT, UniPAD) using consistent training/fine-tuning protocols, including a careful experimental design (fixing fine-tuning iterations at convergence) to avoid conflating pre-training benefit with faster convergence.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains are fairly modest (e.g., +2.48 mAP on NuScenes 5%, ~1.28 average mAP/mAPH gain on Waymo 1%), and the headline claim of '100% more improvement' is a relative comparison between small baseline margins, which can be misleading/sensitive to noise; more statistical rigor (e.g., repeated runs with std) is provided only for a subset of experiments (NuScenes mAP), not consistently across all reported numbers/datasets.

Curvature is computed from the SDF network's own predicted normals while that same network is being jointly trained, creating a chicken-and-egg dependency; the paper only addresses this with an ad hoc warm-up (uniform sampling for a few epochs) rather than a principled analysis of how curvature estimates evolve or their sensitivity to noise beyond a few qualitative visualizations.

Downstream evaluation uses only a single detector architecture per dataset (BEVFusion for NuScenes, CenterPoint for Waymo); testing on additional architectures/backbones would strengthen claims of general applicability.

No direct comparison to a 'full' (non-sampled) joint pre-training baseline to quantify how much performance is lost/gained due to sampling versus using all points/pixels, nor an explicit memory/throughput comparison quantifying the computational savings claimed to motivate the method.

Sensitivity/hyperparameter analysis is limited: no ablation on number of prototypes (NK), loss weighting terms (ωSwAV, ωEM, ωGMM), or the Gram matrix regularization's necessity for preventing collapse (no results without it).

Baselines are re-run with 'the same setting as CLAP' using official implementations, but details of what settings were altered/matched are not fully specified, raising minor reproducibility/fairness concerns.

The paper's contribution is somewhat incremental relative to UniPAD (differentiable rendering backbone) and SwAV (prototype/swapping mechanism), with the main novelty being the combination and adaptation of these components to the joint multimodal setting rather than a fundamentally new technique.
